summary:
Eagle & Columbia: The First Journey Home is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) interactive 3D web experience that shows how Apollo 11 really came back from the Moon. Many people, especially kids, imagine a single rocket that landed and flew home. In reality it took a lunar orbit rendezvous: Columbia waited in orbit, Eagle landed, and to return Eagle split in two. Its descent stage became the launch pad and was abandoned at Tranquility Base, where it still stands today. The ascent stage was left in lunar orbit, and only the command capsule came home.

Viewers follow 13 short chapters built on real NASA data: the LRO Moon, the real terrain of Tranquility Base, mission timing, and original Apollo 11 radio audio and transcripts. Between chapters they must tap the right spacecraft part to continue, so the animation becomes a game that teaches. Every part shows what it did and where it ended up. By bringing this abandoned hardware back to life, the project shows that coming home was the hardest part, and why it is not forgotten.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Eagle & Columbia runs in any web browser with nothing to install.

It works like an interactive documentary: a guided 3D animation in 13 chapters, from lunar orbit to the trip home, with short narration, real radio captions and a mission clock. At any moment the viewer can rotate the camera, zoom in and click any spacecraft part to see what it is, how it works, its real specs and its fate: returned to Earth, still on the Moon, or abandoned in orbit. An exploded view shows how Eagle splits in two, and an orbit map shows why a lower orbit catches up. Between chapters the story stops and asks a question. To continue, the viewer must find and tap the right part (for example: "Which half of Eagle stays on the Moon forever?"). Hints appear if needed.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

It explains a little-known part of Apollo: the trip back, and the hardware that was left behind to make it possible. It is free, bilingual and designed for all ages, at home or in a classroom. We want people to come away knowing that there was no single rocket, and that Apollo 11 left real machines on and around the Moon. Some of them, like the laser retroreflector, are still used today.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- JavaScript, HTML and CSS: the web app and its interface.

- three.js (WebGL): real-time 3D graphics.

- GLSL shaders: a realistic Moon rendered from NASA LRO imagery and elevation data, plus the real Tranquility Base terrain.

- Web Audio API and Web Speech API: synthesized in-cabin sounds and narration.

- Python (NumPy, Pillow): processing NASA data (textures, terrain model, star catalog, audio).

- GitHub Pages: free public hosting.

- Claude (Anthropic): SI assistant for code and text, disclosed inside the app.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most people never wonder how the astronauts got home from the Moon. We turned that question into a playable story: you don't just watch the mission, you have to use what you learned to unlock the next chapter. Real NASA audio, transcripts and terrain make it feel authentic, and every abandoned piece of hardware becomes a character with its own story.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Suitable for all ages; simple, clear language; accuracy (mission numbers come from NASA sources and approximations are labelled); attractive, realistic visuals; an engaging rhythm; interaction that requires knowledge to move forward; two languages; and it runs on ordinary computers (adaptive quality) and even offline.
